what_its_for: Bedaquiline is an antibiotic used to treat a serious type of tuberculosis (TB) called multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). It is always used together with other TB medicines — never alone. It works by stopping the TB bacteria from making the energy they need to survive and grow.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets whole with water. Always take bedaquiline WITH food, as food helps your body absorb the medicine much better. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Never stop taking this medicine or any of your other TB medicines without talking to your doctor first, even if you start to feel better.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take. The usual adult schedule is: Weeks 1–2: Take 400 mg (four 100 mg tablets) once a day. Weeks 3–24: Take 200 mg (two 100 mg tablets) three times a week, with at least 48 hours between doses (for example, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday). The total treatment course is 24 weeks. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: During Weeks 1–2 (daily dosing): If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next scheduled dose as planned. Do not double up. During Weeks 3–24 (three-times-a-week dosing): Take the missed dose as soon as you remember, then continue your regular three-times-a-week schedule. Never take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store bedaquiline at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C and 30°C). Keep the tablets in their original bottle with the cap tightly closed. Keep away from moisture, heat, and direct sunlight. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use past the expiration date printed on the bottle.
what_to_avoid: Avoid alcohol while taking bedaquiline, as it can increase the risk of serious heart side effects. Avoid taking St. John's Wort (an herbal supplement) because it can make bedaquiline much less effective. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially heart rhythm medicines, antifungal medicines (like ketoconazole), HIV medicines, or other antibiotics. Some medicines can interact with bedaquiline and cause dangerous heart problems.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: Fainting or passing out. Fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat or chest pain. Severe nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems). Unusual tiredness or weakness. Feeling dizzy or lightheaded. Any new or worsening symptoms. You will need regular electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG) tests and blood tests during treatment to check your heart and liver — do not skip these appointments.
when_it_works: Bedaquiline starts working against the TB bacteria right away, but you may not feel better for several weeks. It is very important to complete the full 24-week course of treatment even if you feel well. Stopping early can allow the TB bacteria to come back stronger and harder to treat.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Use only if clearly needed, as the risks to the baby are not fully known. Children: Bedaquiline is approved for children 5 years and older weighing at least 15 kg (about 33 lbs). Doses are lower for children — your doctor will calculate the right dose. Older adults (65+): Use with caution. Your doctor may monitor you more closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease before starting this medicine, as dose adjustments or extra monitoring may be needed.
